notable_absence.finding: Two gaps, one of them the batch's most interesting. (1) NO CARDINALITY VOCABULARY. 'Each index is created on one keyspace (collection) only; but multiple indexes may be created on a single keyspace' is a complete 1:N statement in one sentence, and the registry cannot express either half of it. Nine rounds of reference extraction never needed arity because a statement either has a clause or it does not; a deployed system is full of one-of-these-per-that facts (1 service instance per node, max 7 services per node, 1 KV Engine per bucket, 1 keyspace per index, N indexes per keyspace, at least 1 Data node per cluster). Across this batch I minted requiresMinimumNodeCount, instantiatedPerBucket and scopedToKeyspace as three separate ad hoc dodges around the same missing capability; reconciliation should probably replace all three with one cardinality construct rather than promote them individually. (2) NO CO-RESIDENCY PREDICATE. The Index Service's Projector and Router runs on Data Service nodes, so the Index Service physically occupies nodes it was never assigned to. This breaks the tidy 'services are placed on nodes' model that services.md presents, and no registry predicate could state it. I omitted nothing for lack of evidence on this page. I did NOT attempt to model the Projector-and-Router mutation pipeline (Data Service streams -> Projector extracts per index-definition -> sends to Supervisor -> index populated -> then continuous mutation flow) as relations, because it is a sequence with a before/after phase change ('Prior to the creation of any indexes, the **Projector and Router** takes no action'), and the registry has no ordering or state-transition predicate. That is the third page in this batch to hit the missing-sequence gap.

cross_component_finding: (1) ANCHOR/TITLE MISMATCH, a concrete docs bug: the section renders as 'Primary and Global Secondary Indexes' but its anchor is '#using-global-secondary-indexes'. Any external deep link built from the title will not resolve, and any link built from the anchor is mislabeled. (2) CONTENT DUPLICATION, three-way. This page's 'Primary and Global Secondary Indexes' section and indexes.md's Primary/Secondary entries state the same two definitions in different words, and indexes.md links back HERE for both of them - so the reader is bounced between two pages that each partially define the same thing. Meanwhile the 'Saving Indexes' section restates the Enterprise/Community storage split that storage-modes.md documents in full (the 7.2 extraction of this page recorded the same duplication, so it has survived at least one release). (3) The Community/Enterprise storage paragraphs are not parallel: the Community bullet describes write modes, the Enterprise bullet describes compaction plus a 7.0 file-layout change. They read as two unrelated facts under one heading rather than a comparison, which made behavesDifferentlyUnder the only usable predicate even though the two objects are not really being contrasted. (4) 'Supervisor' appears capitalised as a proper component name in the architecture section but lowercase as 'The supervisor process' in the Standard storage description - minor, but the kind of inconsistency that defeats automated term extraction.
cross_product_finding: This page and indexes.md are the two canonical conceptual sources for the index area, and between them they touch only a fraction of the ~93 index-related ids the corpus has accumulated. Specifically: NEITHER PAGE MENTIONS INDEX STATE AT ALL. The registry's index-state ConceptScheme (scheduled for creation / deferred / building / pending / online / offline / abridged) and capella:index-ui-status (ready / pause / warmup) have no anchor whatsoever in the conceptual documentation - both are artifacts of reference and UI material, and nothing in server/'s learn tree tells a reader that an index HAS a lifecycle. That is a documentation gap as much as an ontology one. Conversely this page contributes an axis the reference tree never named as such: index STORAGE MODE (standard vs memory-optimized), which is a property of the service configuration, not of an individual index, and is edition-gated. So the two trees are not merely differently detailed, they are differently sliced.
